title: Would you compel them?
hookLine: had your Lord willed, all would believe, so would you compel people (10:99)
tomorrow: The surah that turned him gray

lines: THE PROPHET FELT THE PULL TOO.
cards: A parent and a grown child at the same table, seeing the world two different ways. Or two old friends. One of them is sure, and can see exactly how much easier the other's life would be with a little agreement.
Then comes the push. One more article. One more argument at dinner.
The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ felt that pull about his own people in Mecca: his neighbors, his relatives, the clan he grew up in. The Qur'an says elsewhere he nearly wore himself out with grief over them.
And right after yesterday's town, Surah Yunus asks him a question.

teach.h: IF GOD WILLED, ALL WOULD BELIEVE.
teach.b: Verse ninety-nine, in Pickthall's translation: "And if thy Lord willed, all who are in the earth would have believed together. Wouldst thou (Muhammad) compel men until they are believers?" Read the first half slowly.
If God wanted a world where everyone believed, He could have had one. He didn't make that world. He made a world where people choose.
And then the question, aimed at the messenger, who had every reason to push: would you compel them?

teach.h: K-R-H — TO FORCE AGAINST THE WILL.
teach.b: The Arabic verb is tukrihu, from the root k-r-h, to force someone into what they dislike. The same root gives a line from al-Baqarah, which Pickthall renders: "There is no compulsion in religion."

teach.h: CONVEY IT; THE REST IS GOD'S.
teach.b: The next verse, one hundred, adds that no soul believes except by God's leave. Belief is not something one person can install in another. Commentators read verse ninety-nine as comfort as much as instruction.
The Prophet's task was to convey the message clearly. What people did with it was between them and God. That lifted a weight he couldn't have carried anyway.
Scholars across the centuries have discussed how this principle sits beside the Qur'an's verses about war and law, and they've debated the details.
But the question in this verse is still asked plainly, and it's addressed to the Prophet himself.
If the one who brought the message wasn't to force it, the line runs through everyone who loves someone and disagrees with them.

how: Muslim scholars cite 10:99 alongside 2:256, 'there is no compulsion in religion,' when teaching that faith must be freely chosen and that a believer's task is to convey the message, not to force it.

o: forcing someone into what they don't want
a promise made to God in a hard time
sharing your faith gently with a neighbor

games.q: inside the question — tap the pairs.
p: no soul believes except by God's leave

s: 10:99 says God could have made everyone believe
if thy Lord willed, all who are in the earth would have believed together.
the question in 10:99 is addressed to unbelievers
it's addressed to the Prophet himself: would you compel them?
'no compulsion in religion' is in Surah Yunus
it's in al-Baqarah, 2:256; it shares its root, k-r-h, with today's verse.

games.q: you've brought a message you know is true, and the people you love most won't accept it. the Qur'an asks you a question. what is it?
o: would you compel them until they believe?
why not leave them for good?
games.why: would you compel them? the verse reminds the Prophet that if God had willed, all would believe; his task was to convey.

practice: Bring to mind one person you keep trying to change: their politics, their habits, their faith or their lack of it.
Notice the push in you, the speech you've half rehearsed, and for now, put it down and let them be exactly who they are. If you pray, you can pray for them, and leave the rest with God.

wordCard.voice: Compulsion. The Qur'an's question to the Prophet in 10:99: if God had willed, all would believe, so belief is not to be forced, there is no compulsion in religion. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: "would you then compel people?" from 10:99; tukrihu is from k-r-h, to force.

carryVoice: Your line: not by force. Conveying is yours; the rest is God's. Until next time.

sources.q: And if thy Lord willed, all who are in the earth would have believed together. Wouldst thou (Muhammad) compel men until they are believers?
There is no compulsion in religion.
